tei:titleStmt.tei:title: אֵל אֲשֶׁר חַסְדּוֹ - פיוט על תפילת חנה
El Asher Ḥasdo — Prayer of Ḥannah, a piyyuṭ for Rosh Hashanah by the Diwan Ashira Project

tei:div.tei:head: El Asher Ḥasdo — Prayer of Ḥannah, a piyyuṭ for Rosh Hashanah by the Diwan Ashira Project

tei:lg.tei:l: O Lord, who does not withhold His kindness,
Who among His people does reside
To be sanctified by the mouths of His multitudes:
Train my lips to pray like those of Ḥannah!
O Merciful One, console my bitter soul,
Allow it only to serve You with joy,
For it is not wine that stupefies
My soul, grieving like that of Ḥannah.
Alone I stand
And ask “May I succeed!”;
My soul thirsts with desire
To encounter You, as did Ḥannah.
Not with shouts and loud cries
Shall I beg You to incline your ear,
Rather, it is a tormented soul You hear,
Like the whispering heart of Ḥannah.
Embrace and accept my offering,
The clear words of my tongue,
Like the voice of the Levites’ song
And the rustle of the lips of Ḥannah.
“Swiftly unfold over us
A canopy of peace!”
That is the wish that I admit,
Like the heartful prayer of Ḥannah.

tei:note.tei:p: Find Genesis 27:27
Find Exodus 25:8, Exodus 29:45
The presence of an edah (congregation) is required for the recitation of “sacred words.” Find Berachot 21b, Megillah 23b
Per Jeremiah 14:10, a people accustomed to traveling.
An allusion to the statement of Rav Hamnuna in Berakhot 31a: “How many great halakhot can be learned from the verses of Ḥannah’s prayer!”
According to Ḥannah’s self-description in I Samuel 1:10
Prayer is called “work that is in the heart” in Tractate Ta’anit 2:1
So that she may succeed in praying to You with joy, as stated in the Baraita: One does not stand to pray [...] except with the joy of a mitsvah (Berakhot 31a).

An allusion to the halakhah that a drunk person is forbidden to pray, which is learned (in Berakhot there) from Eli’s description of Ḥannah’s prayer in I Samuel. This expression is taken from the verse “and drunk, but not with wine” (Isaiah 51:21) and means to lose one’s mind as a result of distress.
Ibid I Samuel 1:10
Alone by myself, an allusion to the words of the Gemara that it is forbidden to sit within four cubits of a person who is praying (Berakhot 31b).
to pray, as Ḥannah said in relation to her prayer: “I am the woman who stands here before you praying” (I Samuel 1:26).
According to Psalms 118:25
According to Psalms 42:3
In the style of baqashah and tefilah (in plea and prayer)
From whose prayer the Gemara learned the halakhah mentioned above on praying alone (ibid Berakhot).
A reference to the biblical story of the confrontation between Eliyahu and the prophets of Baal in 1 Kings 18:26-29. Those who were not answered were those who called to their god with a loud voice.
The style of Daniel’s prayer in Daniel 9:18
An allusion to the halakhah that one should not pray aloud, which is learned in Berachot 31a from the description of Ḥannah’s prayer in 1 Samuel 1:13.
An allusion to the halakhah that the words of prayer must be pronounced correctly (“cut with the lips”), which is learned in Berachot 26b from the description of the verses about Hannah’s prayer.

A reference to the context in which Ḥannah prayed at the Mishkan. The sacrificial service is the model according to which the three daily prayers were designed, according to Rabbi Joshua ben Levi (Berakhot 26b), as it is said: “And we will pay with our lips” (Hosea 14:3), finds only a hinted expression here, in words borrowed from the verse “Accept, O Lord, the offerings of my lips” (Psalms 119:108). Instead, the prayer is attributed here to the singing of the Levites.
according to the description of the verse that is the source of this halakha: “Only her lips were moving” (I Samuel 1:13).
From the prayer, “Hashkivenu”. This piyyut ends, like many other piyyutim, with hope and prayer.

I will wait and speak with intention, as Ḥannah spoke from her heart, as described in the verse “And Ḥannah speaks from her heart” (I Samuel 1:13), from which the Gemara learns that one must pray with intention (Berakhot 26b).
